purpose: Review direct stomach-content evidence for Johnius borneensis in two Western Central Pacific estuaries. Compare study methods, life-stage and locality scope, then retain the records as comparative evidence without presenting either as a Caraga or Philippines-specific diet.

studySources.citation: Simanjuntak, C. P. H., Kustiyani, K., Affandi, R., Rahardjo, M. F., and Prabowo, T. (2022). Feeding preferences and diet overlap of sciaenids fishes in Pabean Bay, Indramayu. Jurnal Iktiologi Indonesia, 22(2), 157-175. https://doi.org/10.32491/jii.v22i2.652
studySources.studyArea: Pabean Bay estuary, Indramayu, West Java, Indonesia; estuary associated with the Cimanuk River and Java Sea.

sampling.gear: Sero/fish trap and bottom gill nets with several mesh sizes.
sampling.dietMethod: Stomachs were dissected and examined with a stereomicroscope; prey items were separated, measured by volume and identified morphologically to the lowest possible taxon.
sampling.sampleCountMeaning: The paper's Table 1 reports 26 captured J. borneensis; the number of this species' non-empty stomachs or stomachs actually included in the diet calculation is not separately stated in the reviewed text.
sampling.lengthRangeMm: 121-290 total length as reported in the paper.

dietResults.index: Index of Preponderance (Ii), as reported by the authors; these are index values, not percentages of fish or directly interchangeable with %IRI.
dietResults.interpretation: The authors describe decapod crustaceans, especially Penaeus sp., as the leading food items for this sample. Sillago sp. is a low-index fish prey item in their table.

reuse.license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0), stated on the article page.
reuse.decision: Retain a limited attributed research summary only. Do not copy tables, article figures or substantial text. Because the license is non-commercial, product-level reuse remains subject to review if Bangwit is used commercially.

studySources.citation: Soe, K. K., Hajisamae, S., Sompongchaiyakul, P., Towatana, P., and Pradit, S. (2022). Feeding Habits and the Occurrence of Anthropogenic Debris in the Stomach Content of Marine Fish from Pattani Bay, Gulf of Thailand. Biology, 11(2), 331. https://doi.org/10.3390/biology11020331
studySources.studyArea: Off the mouth of Pattani Bay, lower Gulf of Thailand; fish were sampled along 2 m, 4 m and 6 m depth contours.

sampling.period: 13 monthly sampling rounds, February 2019 through February 2020.
sampling.dietMethod: Stomachs were opened and identifiable prey in non-empty stomachs were counted and identified to the lowest possible taxon; %IRI and average food types were calculated.
sampling.feedingGuild: Zoobenthivore; the authors define this guild as feeding mainly on polychaetes.

dietResults.index: % Index of Relative Importance (%IRI), as reported by the authors; not percent body mass or proportion of individual fish.
dietResults.variation: Average food-type count for J. borneensis varied significantly by sampled depth and season in this study (Table 1); the result does not establish a particular direction of change or apply to a Philippine waterbody.

reuse.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated in the publisher PDF/article record.
reuse.decision: Retain a factual attributed summary and citation; do not copy the table or figures. Public app admission still needs product-level provenance and presentation review.

comparison.finding: The sampled Pabean Bay fish showed a strong crustacean signal led by Penaeus sp.; the Pattani Bay dataset classified J. borneensis as zoobenthivorous and reported polychaetes as its largest %IRI category, alongside fish, shrimp and other benthos.
comparison.interpretation: These studies demonstrate that a species-level diet label needs locality, period, sampling method, size/stage and source context. Differences between the two samples do not by themselves identify the cause; habitat, prey availability, season, fish size, sampling and index methods may differ.
comparison.PhilippineApplicability: Comparative only. Neither study sampled the Philippines, Caraga or Pagatpatan. These results do not establish prey availability or diet composition for a Philippine population.

limitations: The two studies concern different estuaries in Indonesia and Thailand and cannot substitute for local Philippine diet sampling.
Pabean Bay reports 26 captured J. borneensis but not a separately verifiable count of stomachs used in its species-level diet calculation.
The Pabean study uses Index of Preponderance values, while Pattani reports %IRI; these statistics are not directly interchangeable.
The studies differ in period, gear, sample size, prey classification and likely habitat; the comparison does not prove why their diet profiles differ.
A diet summary is not a bait suggestion, catchability estimate, legal fishing recommendation, current-presence record or safety advisory.
No exact Philippine prey taxa, species-level Philippine diet, or local population inference is added.
One source is CC BY-NC 4.0; future commercial use of that source's protected content requires separate review.
nextAction: Search Philippine primary studies that sampled Johnius borneensis in named estuaries and inspect whether stomach or prey data were measured. If none are located in the bounded search, keep the diet profile comparative-only and proceed with the next regional habitat/species evidence review.
